To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
medial septum (MS) but not mammillary body ( MB) radio-frequency lesions disrupt memory performance in a delayed-matching-to-position (DMTP) task.
rats with lesions of the medial septum (MS) show increased forgetting rates in a delayed matching to sample task, and that this impairment does not appear to be mediated by proactive interference.
rats with MS lesions showed impaired memory performance in a delayed-matching-to-place task, whereas rats with MB lesions showed normal memory performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the medial septum in memory processes, and in particular with its involvement in the encoding and retrieval of spatial information.
how the hippocampal formation is involved in memory processes.
the neural mechanisms underlying memory function in rats and the effects of brain damage on memory function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the MS region is important to memory performance in a DMTS procedure, but this effect is best characterized as a rate-of-forgetting deficit rather than an impairment in the ability to discriminate between stimuli.
MS lesions impair memory performance, but MB lesions do not.
MS lesions impair DMTS performance by increasing the rate of forgetting, whereas MB lesions do not affect DMTS performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MS lesions disrupt memory performance through an impairment in memory retention and not by disrupting the ability to respond to proactive interference.
the hippocampal-MS system is involved in the encoding, consolidation, and retrieval of memory, and that the hippocampus and MS are differentially involved in these processes.
the MS region is necessary for memory function, but not through the mechanism of proactive interference.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mammillary body region is not critical for DMTS performance.
the MS and MB lesions have different effects on memory performance.
the mammillary body is not involved in forgetting.
